issues.legal_issue: An accused in a criminal complaint proceeding may submit relevant, legally admissible documents to establish that a statutory sanction is required, even after process has been issued and before the accused may lead evidence on the merits.
material_facts: A magistrate issued process against public officials on a complaint and supporting evidence alleging assault and other offences.

After appearing, the officials asserted that the alleged acts were done in the discharge or purported discharge of official duties and relied on documents in support of their request to recall process.
The issue was considered as a bar to the court’s jurisdiction to take cognizance, rather than as a defence on the merits of the complaint.
issues.conclusion: An accused is not barred from producing relevant documentary material that can be legally considered without formal proof, for the limited purpose of deciding whether the sanction requirement applies.
issues.legal_principle: Section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure bars cognizance without prior government sanction when its requirements are met. The sanction question concerns the court’s jurisdiction and is distinct from a merits defence; it may be considered at any stage and on relevant materials then available. The Court relied on Matajog Dobey v. H.C. Bhari, which held that the need for sanction may emerge as the case progresses; S.B. Saha, which permits consideration of materials on the record when the question arises; and Pukhraj v. State of Rajasthan, which likewise recognized that the question may depend on the stage of the case. It distinguished the limits on considering an accused’s merits defence before trial.

predicates.criminal_complaint_proceeding: A criminal complaint is being considered by a magistrate and process has been issued against the accused.
predicates.accused_raises_official_duty_sanction_ba: The accused asserts that the alleged acts were done or purportedly done in official duty and that prior sanction is required.
predicates.accused_submits_relevant_admissible_docu: The accused submits documents relevant to that assertion that can be considered without formal proof.

issues.definition: When an accused in a complaint proceeding raises an official-duty sanction bar and submits relevant admissible documents, the accused may use those documents for the limited determination of whether the bar applies.

issues.legal_issue: Prior sanction is required when the alleged conduct of a public servant who falls within the protected category was done or purportedly done in the discharge of official duty, even if the conduct is alleged to have involved excesses.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that senior district and police officials intervened to prevent municipal staff from removing an unauthorised structure and that officials assaulted and threatened the complainant and others.
The witnesses’ accounts described the officials taking control of the site amid a gathering crowd and tension over the proposed removal.
The alleged conduct was connected to the officials’ intervention in a developing public-order situation; the Court considered it prima facie to have been done or purportedly done in official duties.
The Court left the justification for the conduct and whether the officials committed excesses to be determined at trial after the required sanction was obtained.
issues.conclusion: A case for sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was prima facie made out, so the appeals were dismissed; the Court expressed no opinion on the merits of the allegations.
issues.legal_principle: Section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to a public servant not removable from office save by or with government sanction when the alleged offence concerns an act done or purportedly done in the discharge of official duty. The act need not itself be an official duty, and an alleged excess may still be protected if sufficiently connected with or purportedly undertaken in official duty; an act wholly in a private capacity is not protected. The Court relied on Matajog Dobey v. H.C. Bhari, including its statement that the connection to duty may become apparent as the case progresses, and Pukhraj v. State of Rajasthan, which distinguishes excess in purported official action from conduct having no semblance of official duty. It also relied on S.B. Saha concerning consideration of materials available when the sanction question arises.

predicates.criminal_complaint_proceeding: A criminal complaint proceeding is before a court for consideration of cognizance or continuation of the case.
predicates.protected_public_servant: The accused is a public servant who cannot be removed from office except by or with government sanction.
predicates.alleged_conduct_purports_to_be_official_: The alleged conduct is connected with an act the public servant did or purported to do in carrying out official duties, rather than an act wholly in a private capacity.

issues.definition: If a complaint proceeding concerns a public servant in the protected category and alleges conduct purportedly undertaken in official duty, the proceeding requires prior government sanction.
